explanation: No shared token or context. Top examples are scattered: fixed phrases ('safe to say/assume', 'so as to', 'not only', 'not to mention'), digits inside numbers, commas in lists, name and word-piece tokens, and code. There is no rule that predicts when it fires.

Fires on the argument token right after an opening parenthesis, bracket or angle bracket in code or LaTeX (e.g. '(file' in 'path.resolve(file)', 'g(x', '<T', '.length' inside []), and on the token just before the closing bracket. Strongest on short nested function-call or index arguments. Weak or absent in prose.

Fires on vague or generic referring words in informal news and blog prose that point back to earlier discourse or link to the next point: 'such', 'reason(s)', 'why', 'it', 'stuff', 'all', 'issue', 'result' in 'as a result', and sentence-start connectives like 'Plus', 'Again', 'Like', 'Various'. Weak on content nouns and technical text.

Fires on a technical noun or noun stem that names the main entity of the phrase in scientific, patent or programming text (e.g. 'acid', 'magnet', 'lead', 'effector', 'complex', 'polymer', 'packet', 'class', 'tab'), often right after a determiner or modifier. Generic everyday nouns give only weak activation.

Fires on a word-piece inside a rare or technical multi-token word or name (e.g. 'stigm', 'sediment', '[3H]', 'Petal-UM-a', 'Riksbank', 'immunoph') and on dots inside version numbers or dotted identifiers. Driven mainly by being partway through an unusual word, not by meaning.

Fires on an abstract noun or function word that sets up an upcoming clause in expository prose, e.g. 'the choice', 'the only difference', 'the challenge', 'several advantages', 'our aim', 'no reason', 'two ways', 'already', 'previous', 'most of', 'at the end of'. Strongest on frame nouns that ask for what follows. Weak on commas and plain function words.

Mixed. Fires on word-final suffix pieces ('-ed', '-ing', '-ments', '-ish'), domain endings ('.org', '.net'), 'you' in the GPL license line 'This program is free software; you can', and pieces of non-English words. The examples share no clear concept.

Fires most strongly on the closing parenthesis after a birth date (or birth-death dates) in a Wikipedia biography opening, e.g. 'Name (born 29 May 2004[)] is a ...'. Weaker, scattered activations come from code tokens and verbs that follow 'to' or 'had' in prose.

Fires on the second half of a hyphenated compound adjective or participle, especially '-modified', '-catalyzed', '-labeled', '-infected', '-acquired', '-linked', '-issued', '-coated' (X-ed form). Also fires on '-ged' in 'flagged' and on '-in' compounds. Strongest in chemistry and biomedical text.

Mixed. Fires on commas inside numbers and in diff hunk headers, on word-pieces in the middle of multi-token words ('Lactoc-occus', 'quick-cou-pling', 'Sperm-ato'), on list items after commas (element symbols, initials), on hyphens in 'mid-1980', and on assorted prose words. There is no clear single trigger.

Two jobs. (1) Clause-ending commas in narrative or expository prose that come after a complete phrase, before the main or continuing clause (e.g. 'Based on ... tweeted[,] it sounds'). (2) The middle word-piece of certain Latin-derived scientific words, especially 'Dipt-era' or 'visc-era', 'Acc-umb-ens', 'evis-cer-ate'. Commas inside lists or numbers fire only weakly.

Fires on function words and verb or preposition tokens in the middle of formal or descriptive phrases, often after a verb or adjective and before its complement (e.g. 'SUM [Of]', 'considered [to]', 'designed [for]/[to]', 'referred [to]', 'banned from use [in]', '(b) [Description]', 'The [following]'). The context is broad and there is no sharp lexical trigger.

Mixed. Fires on code tokens such as '__name__', 'function', '$_POST', '.length', and indentation before 'public' after @Override. It also fires on prose words like 'quite', 'blame', 'hours', 'Fixtures', 'reel'. Mostly a code-syntax detector with unrelated prose hits.

Fires in historical or biographical narration on the word that finishes a beginning, founding or transition phrase: the space before a year after 'opened in', 'founded in', 'started in'; 'since its [inception]', 'dawn [of]', 'parted [ways]', 'set [out]', 'fallen [into]', 'retiring [as]', 'elected ... [to]'. Strongest on phrases about origins or changes of state.

Fires on assorted function words and nouns in explanatory or quantitative prose, often inside a comparison, condition or measurement frame (e.g. 'want [if]', 'above [the]', 'name for [the]', 'once [in]', 'the [remainder]', '16% [of]', 'youngest person [to]'). There is no consistent token or semantic trigger.

Fires on the standalone space token right before a number, the kind that number-splitting tokenizers produce (e.g. 'seek[ ]25 years', 'email you[ ]4 weeks', 'directed by[ ]', 'in[ ]2016'). Strongest when the number is a count or quantity in running prose. Weaker before years in dates, before code constants, and on hyphens or digits inside chemical names.

Fires on adjective-forming suffixes and on whole relational or classifying adjectives in academic, scientific or medical text: '-al', '-ological', '-ographic', '-istic', '-ural', '-actic', and words like 'surgical', 'regulatory', 'constitutional', 'depressive', 'educational' that modify a following noun. General or everyday adjectives fire weakly.

Mixed. Fires strongly on 'even' as a scalar intensifier ('didn't even know', 'never even'), and also on assorted nouns and adjectives in descriptive prose ('dilation', 'stage', 'typical', 'cause', 'competing', 'prototype', 'details', 'important') with no unifying context.

Mostly fires on the subject 'we' in academic abstracts after 'Here' or 'Here,' ('Here we report/show'), and on 'is'/'was' after 'The aim/objective of this work'. These are the abstract sentences that state the purpose of the study. A few unrelated hits come from names, code and commas.

Mixed. Fires on 'by' after a methods verb ('isolated by', 'determined by'), on commas in lists of technical terms, on '%' in '95% CI', and on code punctuation ('/v', '.', ':'). It also fires on assorted words in scientific-methods and code text, with no single trigger.

Fires on degree adverbs that modify a following adjective, adverb or quantifier: 'pretty', 'too', 'very', 'fairly', and 'mai' in Romanian 'cel mai'. Weaker on 'extremely', 'quite', 'more', 'rather' and 'such'. The token itself is the trigger, and its use as an intensifier matters.
